metadata.note: The Illinois Central's own Chicago–St. Louis route — 294 miles by way of Kankakee, Gilman, Gibson City, Clinton, Springfield and Litchfield — and the Green Diamond that ran it. This was the IC's answer to the Chicago & Alton on the corridor, put together out of the Gilman, Clinton & Springfield (bought 1877) and the St. Louis, Peoria & Northern (bought 1899) and opened to passengers on 17 June 1900. Added 2026-08-27; the IC's Chicago–New Orleans main line was already on the map, but this second Illinois main line was not. Two features on shared geometry: the full Chicago–St. Louis line to 1968, and the cut-back Chicago–Springfield Governor's Special that outlived it to 1971.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Every headway_min in this file is an estimate; no Illinois Central public timetable was consulted. The 1947 re-equipping date and the 1958 consolidation are taken from a single account and have not been cross-checked. Whether any local passenger service ran on the Gilman–Springfield line between the 1877 purchase and the 1900 through service is not established, so nothing is drawn before 1900.
metadata.source: Wikipedia (Illinois Central Railroad, Green Diamond, Gilman Clinton and Springfield Railroad), american-rails.com, Trains Magazine, abandonedrails.com, chicagorailfan.com

properties.speed_source: Partly computed: the Green Diamond's own schedule was 294.2 miles in 4 hours 55 minutes, an average of 59.8 mph (96 km/h) including seven stops. 80 km/h is used here as a blend across 1900–1968, since the pre-1936 trains were slower; the blend itself is an estimate.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap, with labelled approximations at the south end. The Chicago-to-Farmersville two-thirds is real track used verbatim: the ways named 'Chicago Subdivision' and 'CN Gilman Subdivision' that still carry old_railway_operator=IC chain cleanly, the Gilman Subdivision alone running an unbroken 136.9 miles. That spine is also the check that the trace is on the right railroad: the Gilman, Clinton & Springfield was a documented 111 miles from Gilman to Springfield, and the subdivision continues about 26 miles beyond Springfield to Farmersville, which adds up. APPROXIMATED LEGS: south of Farmersville the ex-IC Springfield District is largely lifted, surviving only as disconnected rail-trail (the MCT Heritage trails through Glen Carbon and Edwardsville) and scattered abandoned right-of-way. Of the 10 joins needed along the whole route, 7 are routed on real track and 3 are STRAIGHT LINES totalling 23.3 km, every one of them in that Litchfield-to-Glen Carbon stretch: 8.71 km near [-89.7276, 39.0725]; 10.05 km near [-89.7912, 39.0117]; 4.54 km near [-89.8434, 38.9309]. Traced length 300.4 miles against the 294.2 route miles the Green Diamond's own schedule documents. Three out-and-back excursions totalling 8.4 km were detected by the repo's revisit test and removed after routing (5.83 km, 1.29 km, 1.33 km), which is what brings the figure down from 305.7 miles. Three residual reversals under 400 m remain, at Edwardsville and in the East St. Louis terminal area, where the routing crosses junction and yard trackage; they are small enough to be junction geometry rather than spikes, but they have not been hand-cleaned. CAVEAT (CLAUDE.md Rule 2): modern alignment drawn back to 1900, and the St. Louis terminal approach is today's, not the 1900 one. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 5 ruled segments totalling 107 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The Illinois Central's own Chicago–St. Louis line, assembled from two purchases. In July 1877 it bought the Gilman, Clinton & Springfield — 111 miles from Gilman, on the Chicago–Cairo main line, to Springfield via Clinton. In 1899 it bought the St. Louis, Peoria & Northern, which had itself been stitched together from three companies that built Springfield to Mount Olive (1887), on to Alhambra (1889) and into Glen Carbon (1893). Freight ran through on 1 December 1899, and on 17 June 1900 the IC put on the Daylight Special and the Diamond Special to compete with the Chicago & Alton, which had had the corridor to itself. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1877 Gilman, Clinton & Springfield purchase, the 1887/1889/1893 construction of the Springfield–Glen Carbon line, the 1899 St. Louis, Peoria & Northern purchase and the 17 June 1900 inauguration of the Daylight Special and Diamond Special are carried by the references below; the headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: The Green Diamond entered service on 17 May 1936, an articulated streamliner and the IC's flagship on this route: 294.2 miles in 4 hours 55 minutes, an average of 59.8 mph, with stops at 63rd Street (Woodlawn), Kankakee, Gibson City, Clinton, Springfield, Litchfield and East St. Louis. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 17 May 1936 start, the 294.2-mile distance, the 4h55m schedule and the stop list are carried by the references below; the headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: In 1947 conventional equipment with more seats replaced the original articulated Green Diamond trainset, which had been running the route unchanged for eleven years. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1947 re-equipping is carried by the references below; the headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: From 1958 the Green Diamond was the Illinois Central's only Chicago–St. Louis passenger train. On 20 May 1968 the IC cut it back to Springfield and renamed it the Governor's Special, and St. Louis lost its Illinois Central passenger service. headway_min of 720 stands for one train each way per day and is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the 1958 consolidation and the 20 May 1968 truncation and renaming are carried by the references below; the headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: The Governor's Special was what the Green Diamond became on 20 May 1968 when the Illinois Central cut it back from St. Louis to Springfield. It ran the remaining Chicago–Springfield leg until 30 April 1971, the last day before Amtrak; the IC's Springfield line was not in Amtrak's opening network, and the Chicago–St. Louis trains went to the parallel ex-Alton route instead. headway_min of 1440 stands for one train each way per day and is an estimate.
